# More with Less: Efficient Parallel Scientific Code Translation via an Agent-Skill Workflow

Jianuo Shen¹, Pengyi Xu² and Bo Zhang²
Affiliation: ¹csjianuo.shen@mail.scut.edu.cn  
¹ Department of Computer Science & Engineering, South China University
of Technology, Guangzhou, Guangdong 510006 Affiliation: ²{vxu,
bo.zhang}@mtu.edu  
² Department of Computer Science, Michigan Technological University,
Houghton, Michigan 49931

###### Abstract

Translating parallel scientific codes between HPC programming frameworks
is a critical but labor-intensive task. Existing LLM-based approaches
rely on fixed sequential pipelines with undifferentiated repair
strategies and correctness criteria that do not match scientific
computing practice. We present an agent-skill framework that separates
translation, compilation diagnosis, and execution validation into three
autonomous agents coordinated by a verdict-driven orchestrator, routing
each failure to a targeted repair skill rather than retrying blindly. An
automated output check drives the self-correction loop, complemented by
an offline LLM-based verification that exposes false positives escaping
compiler and runtime checks. We evaluate the framework on 30 HeCBench
kernels translated bidirectionally among CUDA, OpenMP, and SYCL with
three open-source LLMs. Our framework attains the higher verified
correctness rate in all 18 model and direction combinations over a
state-of-the-art baseline while consuming up to 52.4% fewer tokens,
remaining consistent across models and directions without architectural
modification.

###### Index Terms: 

Large Language Models, Agentic Workflow, Parallel Code Translation,
Agent-Skill Architecture, HPC Programming Models

## I Introduction

The ability to automatically translate code between programming
languages has long been a goal of software engineering research, and
recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have brought it closer
to practical reality. Modern LLMs such as GPT-4 \[[1](#bib.bib1)\],
DeepSeek Coder \[[2](#bib.bib2)\], and Qwen2.5-Coder \[[3](#bib.bib3)\]
demonstrate strong generalization across programming languages, enabling
translation pipelines that combine prompt engineering, compiler
feedback, and iterative repair to achieve compelling results on
general-purpose benchmarks \[[4](#bib.bib4), [5](#bib.bib5)\]. These
capabilities have sparked growing interest in applying LLMs to automate
the translation of real-world codebases, reducing the manual effort
required to port software across language ecosystems and opening new
avenues for code modernization at scale.

Despite this progress, LLM-based code translation remains poorly
understood in the domain of parallel scientific computing.
General-purpose translation pipelines typically assess correctness
through test case passing rates or code similarity
metrics \[[6](#bib.bib6), [7](#bib.bib7)\], criteria that are adequate
for software engineering tasks but insufficient for scientific computing
workloads. Parallel scientific codes impose a stricter and more
domain-specific notion of correctness: numerical outputs must be
equivalent within floating-point tolerance across potentially billions
of arithmetic operations, translated code must genuinely offload
computation to the target device rather than silently falling back to
CPU execution, and results must be deterministic across parallel
runs \[[8](#bib.bib8), [9](#bib.bib9)\]. These requirements are
difficult to satisfy precisely because the semantics of parallelism,
memory hierarchy, and synchronization differ fundamentally across
programming frameworks such as OpenMP \[[10](#bib.bib11)\],
CUDA \[[11](#bib.bib10)\], and SYCL \[[12](#bib.bib12)\], a semantic gap
that has no analog in conventional language-to-language translation and
that general-purpose pipelines are not designed to bridge. Collectively,
these failures remain invisible to evaluation methodologies that stop at
compilation success or surface-level output matching, yet they are
precisely the failures that matter most in scientific computing
practice.

Several systems have recently addressed aspects of this problem, but
share three recurring limitations. First, existing pipelines follow
fixed sequential workflows with no dynamic routing: all errors are
handled identically regardless of their root cause, leading to
unnecessary LLM calls and poor token efficiency.
LASSI \[[13](#bib.bib13)\] exemplifies this pattern, achieving strong
results on bidirectional OpenMP $`\leftrightarrow`$ CUDA translation
with compiler and execution feedback, but applying the same repair
strategy indiscriminately to every failure type. Second, automated
semantic verification remains absent or superficial.
CodeRosetta \[[14](#bib.bib14)\], a purpose-built encoder-decoder
transformer for C++ $`\leftrightarrow`$ CUDA and C++ $`\leftrightarrow`$
Fortran translation, reports 93% functional correctness on a sample of
30 kernels but does not assess numerical equivalence under
floating-point arithmetic, the correctness criterion most critical for
scientific workloads. LASSI similarly relies on manual output inspection
rather than automated output validation. Third, existing pipelines are
token-inefficient by design. LASSI and similar systems such as
UniPar \[[15](#bib.bib15)\] and ParaCodex \[[9](#bib.bib9)\] apply the
same LLM-based repair strategy regardless of error type, incurring
unnecessary token consumption on failures that could be resolved with
targeted, lightweight interventions. This indiscriminate retry behavior
limits practical scalability and increases inference cost without a
corresponding improvement in translation quality.

Inspired by the emerging paradigm of agent-skill decomposition in
autonomous AI systems \[[5](#bib.bib5), [16](#bib.bib16),
[17](#bib.bib17), [18](#bib.bib18)\], we propose an agentic workflow for
parallel scientific code translation that addresses these limitations
through principled separation of concerns. Our framework comprises three
collaborating agents coordinated by an orchestrator: a TranslationAgent
that encapsulates code analysis, memory-aware planning, and
self-reviewing translation; a CompilationAgent that combines compilation
with structured error classification to dynamically route failures to
the appropriate repair strategy; and an ExecutionAgent that
automatically checks output correctness between source and translated
outputs and diagnoses runtime failures including race conditions and
incorrect GPU offloading. Rather than treating every error as a prompt
for blind retry, our orchestrator reads the verdict from each agent and
selects the repair skill best suited to the diagnosed failure mode,
reducing unnecessary LLM calls and improving overall token efficiency.
We evaluate the framework on 30 HeCBench \[[19](#bib.bib32)\] kernels
translated bidirectionally among OpenMP, CUDA, and SYCL with three
recent open-source LLMs, measuring verified correctness and token
consumption against a state-of-the-art baseline, and further audit the
results under a stricter LLM-based complementary verification. Our
results demonstrate that the agent-skill architecture achieves higher
verified correctness than the baseline while reducing token consumption
by up to 52.4%, remaining consistent across three open-source LLMs and
all six translation directions among CUDA, OpenMP, and SYCL without
architectural modification.

This paper makes the following contributions:

- •
  We propose an agent-skill architecture for parallel scientific code
  translation that separates translation, compilation diagnosis, and
  execution validation into three autonomous agents. This separation
  enables verdict-driven routing that targets each repair skill at a
  specific failure mode, reducing unnecessary LLM calls while improving
  correctness through more precise self-correction.
- •
  We introduce an automated output check as a first-class validation
  step, replacing manual output inspection with a quantitative
  correctness signal that drives a dedicated semantic repair loop,
  together with an LLM-based complementary verification that audits
  translated artifacts offline and exposes false positives escaping the
  output check.
- •
  We demonstrate that our framework achieves higher translation
  correctness than LASSI on the same benchmark while reducing token
  consumption by up to 52.4%, establishing that more capable behavior
  does not require more expensive prompting.
- •
  We show that the framework generalizes across OpenMP, CUDA, and SYCL,
  supporting bidirectional translation between multiple HPC parallel
  programming frameworks without architectural changes.

concludes and outlines directions for future work.

## II Related Work

The rapid diversification of HPC hardware has made parallel scientific
code portability one of the most pressing challenges in computational
science. Leadership-class systems such as Frontier, Aurora, and El
Capitan feature heterogeneous CPU-GPU architectures from different
vendors, each requiring distinct parallel programming frameworks to
achieve peak performance \[[20](#bib.bib19)\]. The current TOP500
list \[[21](#bib.bib20)\] includes GPUs from NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel,
driving a proliferation of parallel programming models including OpenMP,
CUDA, SYCL, HIP \[[22](#bib.bib21)\], and Kokkos \[[23](#bib.bib22)\]
that target overlapping but incompatible hardware
ecosystems \[[24](#bib.bib23)\]. Manual porting is prohibitively
expensive, with domain scientists estimating refactoring costs of
upwards of eleven million dollars per 100,000 lines of
code \[[25](#bib.bib24)\], and risks introducing subtle numerical and
performance errors that are difficult to detect and reproduce. These
pressures have driven growing interest in automated approaches to
parallel scientific code translation, motivating the work surveyed
below.

### II-A LLM-Based Code Translation

Automated code translation has a long history in software engineering.
Early approaches relied on rule-based transpilers that applied
hand-coded linguistic rules to map source language constructs to target
language equivalents (as in SYCLomatic \[[26](#bib.bib41)\], the
production CUDA $`\rightarrow`$ SYCL migration tool), followed by
statistical machine translation methods that applied phrase-based models
originally designed for natural language to translate between
programming languages such as Java and C# \[[27](#bib.bib25),
[28](#bib.bib26), [29](#bib.bib27)\]. The emergence of neural models
brought a significant shift: Roziere et al. introduced
TransCoder \[[30](#bib.bib28)\], an unsupervised transformer model that
leverages masked language modeling, denoising autoencoding, and
back-translation to translate between Python, Java, and C++ without
requiring parallel training data. Subsequent work improved upon this
foundation by incorporating automated unit test execution to filter
invalid translations \[[31](#bib.bib29)\] and by injecting code
structure through abstract syntax trees and compiler
representations \[[32](#bib.bib30)\]. With the rise of large language
models, prompt-based approaches have largely supplanted purpose-built
translation models, enabling zero-shot and few-shot translation across a
much wider range of language pairs without task-specific
training \[[4](#bib.bib4)\]. Compiler feedback and iterative repair
loops have emerged as an effective complement to prompting, feeding
compilation and execution errors back to the LLM for
self-correction \[[6](#bib.bib6)\]. Despite these advances,
general-purpose translation systems assess correctness through code
similarity metrics \[[7](#bib.bib7)\] or test case passing
rates \[[6](#bib.bib6)\], criteria that are insufficient for parallel
scientific codes where numerical equivalence and genuine GPU offload are
the relevant correctness standards.

Applying these advances to parallel scientific codes has motivated a
dedicated line of work in the HPC community. Lei et
al. \[[33](#bib.bib31)\] introduced a dataset of manually curated OpenMP
Fortran and C++ code pairs and demonstrated that fine-tuning LLMs on
HPC-specific translation data significantly improves translation quality
over general-purpose baselines. LASSI \[[13](#bib.bib13)\] introduced a
self-correcting pipeline for bidirectional CUDA $`\leftrightarrow`$
OpenMP translation combining self-prompting, static domain knowledge
injection, and iterative compiler and execution feedback, but follows a
fixed sequential workflow that applies the same repair strategy to every
failure type and relies on manual output inspection rather than
automated output verification; its extension
LASSI-EE \[[34](#bib.bib42)\] targets energy-aware refactoring, without
numerical equivalence verification. CodeRosetta \[[14](#bib.bib14)\]
proposed an unsupervised encoder-decoder transformer for C++
$`\leftrightarrow`$ CUDA and C++ $`\leftrightarrow`$ Fortran translation
with training objectives tailored to parallel code semantics, but
evaluates correctness on a small sample of kernels without assessing
numerical equivalence under floating-point arithmetic.
UniPar \[[15](#bib.bib15)\] evaluated fine-tuning, hyperparameter
optimization, and compiler-guided repair for translation among serial
code, CUDA, and OpenMP, improving over off-the-shelf models while
leaving numerical correctness unverified. ParaCodex \[[9](#bib.bib9)\]
introduced profiling-guided agentic planning for serial and CUDA to
OpenMP GPU offload translation, using hotspot analysis and explicit data
movement planning to prevent performance regressions, but focuses on
parallelization rather than bidirectional translation between
established parallel programming frameworks. Evaluation in this space
has primarily relied on kernel-level benchmarks such as
HeCBench \[[19](#bib.bib32)\], which provides over 500 computational
kernels with CUDA, OpenMP, and SYCL implementations. Most recently,
ParEval-Repo \[[35](#bib.bib33)\] extended evaluation to
repository-level HPC translation, finding that existing approaches
largely fail beyond trivial kernel scale due to cross-file dependencies
and build system complexity. Across these systems, three recurring
limitations emerge: fixed sequential workflows with no dynamic
error-type-aware routing, absence of automated correctness verification,
and indiscriminate repair strategies that incur unnecessary token
consumption regardless of failure type.

### II-B Agentic Workflows for Software Engineering

The application of LLM-based agents to software engineering tasks has
grown rapidly, driven by the observation that complex software tasks
require multi-step reasoning, tool use, and iterative self-correction
that single-prompt approaches cannot provide. ReAct \[[5](#bib.bib5)\]
established the foundational paradigm of interleaving reasoning and
acting in LLM-based agents. SWE-agent \[[36](#bib.bib34)\] demonstrated
that agent-computer interfaces enabling LLMs to interact with terminals,
editors, and test runners substantially outperform static prompt-based
approaches on real-world GitHub issue resolution.
AutoCodeRover \[[37](#bib.bib35)\] combined LLMs with AST-based program
analysis to autonomously localize and repair bugs, while
RepairAgent \[[38](#bib.bib36)\] showed that LLM-based agents with
access to compilation and test execution feedback can navigate complex
repair trajectories autonomously. These systems share a common
architectural insight: separating high-level decision-making from
low-level execution enables more robust workflows than monolithic prompt
chains.

Skills as stateless execution units have gained attention for improving
modularity and token efficiency. Rather than routing all tasks through a
single LLM call or distributing them across communicating agents,
skill-based architectures assign lightweight, targeted execution to
specialized stateless components, reducing token usage compared to
multi-agent alternatives \[[18](#bib.bib18)\], while reserving expensive
LLM reasoning for decisions that genuinely require
it \[[16](#bib.bib16)\]. The advantage of dynamic, conditional execution
over fixed sequential pipelines has also been demonstrated directly in
code translation: Gray et al. \[[39](#bib.bib37)\] found that an agentic
MATLAB $`\rightarrow`$ HDL translation pipeline with conditional tool
invocation outperforms fixed sequential workflows by over 20% points,
with gains attributed to short prompts and on-demand tool use. These
agentic software engineering systems, however, assess correctness
through test suite execution, criteria that do not transfer to parallel
scientific codes where numerical equivalence, genuine GPU offload, and
parallel determinism are the relevant correctness standards. Our work
applies the agent-skill paradigm to this domain, introducing
domain-specific correctness verification as a first-class component of
the agentic workflow rather than a post-hoc evaluation step.

## III System Design

![Refer to caption](2611.08947v1/images/system_design.png)

Fig. 1: System overview. The orchestrator drives a verdict-based
self-correction loop through the three agents, routing each diagnosed
failure to a targeted repair skill until the translation passes
compilation and output checking or the self-correction budget is
exhausted.

This section presents the design of our LLM-driven code translation
framework. Translating parallel programs between programming models is
rarely a one-shot task: LLM-generated code frequently fails to compile,
and code that compiles may still produce incorrect results at runtime.
Rather than treating translation as a single generation step, our
framework organizes the task as a multi-agent system in which
specialized agents collaborate through a central orchestrator and an
iterative repair loop. An LLM is invoked for code generation, rewriting,
analysis, and planning tasks. Meanwhile, in-loop verification is
delegated to the real compiler and runtime behavior, complemented by an
offline LLM-based complementary verification.

### III-A Overview and Design Goals

Our framework translates parallel programs between different parallel
programming models through a multi-agent system coordinated by a central
orchestrator. As shown in Figure
[1](#S3.F1 "Fig. 1 ‣ III System Design ‣ More with Less: Efficient Parallel Scientific Code Translation via an Agent-Skill Workflow"),
the system consists of three agents: a TranslationAgent generates the
target-language code, a CompilationAgent validates that the code
compiles, and an ExecutionAgent runs the compiled binary and checks
correctness. Each agent is composed of a fixed set of skills that it
executes in sequence: the TranslationAgent runs code analysis, memory
planning, and translation skills; the CompilationAgent runs compiler
invocation and error classification skills; and the ExecutionAgent runs
binary execution and runtime analysis skills. In addition, the framework
provides specialized repair skills to handle distinct compilation and
runtime failure modes.

The orchestrator drives the workflow through a verdict-based
self-correction loop. After each agent or repair skill executes, the
orchestrator records the returned verdict and consults a routing table
that maps every verdict status to the next agent, a repair skill, or a
terminal state. The loop terminates upon reaching a terminal verdict,
exhausting a global step limit, or exceeding a unified self-correction
budget that counts only repair invocations. This verdict-driven routing
separates the concerns of code generation, failure classification and
repair.

The overarching goal of the framework is to support translation between
arbitrary parallel programming models. To make this practical, concrete
translation logic is encapsulated in dynamically loaded skills rather
than baked into the agent or orchestrator code, so adding a new
source$`\rightarrow`$target translation pair requires only pair-specific
skill implementations and prompts without modifying the system
architecture. The active pair is selected at runtime through a single
configuration flag, which swaps the bound skill implementations, prompt
templates, and compiler choices.

|                  |                      |                                                                                 |                  |                  |
| ---------------- | -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------- | ---------------- |
| Agent            | Skill                | Trigger condition                                                               | Verdict          | Routed to        |
| CompilationAgent | ErrorClassifierSkill | Linker errors (undefined reference, multiple definition, ld failure)            | PATCH            | PatchSkill       |
|                  |                      | Leftover source-framework keywords (e.g., \_\_host\_\_, \_\_device\_\_)         | PATCH            | PatchSkill       |
|                  |                      | Target-framework API or directive misuse (e.g., sycl::, omp target, cudaMalloc) | PATCH            | PatchSkill       |
|                  |                      | Genuine memory-allocation failures (out of memory, invalid device pointer)      | MEMORY           | MemoryRepair     |
|                  |                      | Missing headers or source files                                                 | PATCH            | PatchSkill       |
|                  |                      | C++ syntax, type, or scope errors                                               | PATCH            | PatchSkill       |
|                  |                      | Empty compiler log (no actionable error)                                        | RETRANSLATE      | TranslationAgent |
| ExecutionAgent   | RuntimeAnalysisSkill | Exit code 0 and no FAIL marker in stdout                                        | EQUIVALENT       | Done (terminal)  |
|                  |                      | Exit code 0 but explicit FAIL marker in stdout                                  | SEMANTIC         | SemanticRepair   |
|                  |                      | Non-zero exit code                                                              | CRASH            | SyncRepair       |
|                  |                      | Execution timeout; args auto-scaled and rerun                                   | REPAIR_EXECUTION | RunnerSkill      |

TABLE I: Classification of compilation and runtime failures into verdict
categories.

### III-B Task State, Verdict, and Orchestrator

The framework uses a shared TaskState object to represent the evolving
state of a single translation task as it moves through the
orchestrator’s self-correction loop. Initialized from the source program
and pair configuration, it tracks the current translated code, the
latest compilation and execution artifacts, and bookkeeping information
such as step history and retry counters. A generic metadata bucket
inside the TaskState allows skills to share intermediate context, such
as code summaries and memory plans. Both agents and skills mutate this
state in place, which simplifies the communication protocol.

Agents and skills communicate through a structured Verdict object that
encodes the outcome of the most recent step. The orchestrator invokes
CompilationAgent or ExecutionAgent, which maps compiler log or runtime
output to a verdict category according to a set of trigger conditions.
The orchestrator then dispatches the verdict to the corresponding repair
skill or back to TranslationAgent via a fixed routing table. The mapping
from trigger conditions to verdicts and their routing targets is given
in
Table [I](#S3.T1 "TABLE I ‣ III-A Overview and Design Goals ‣ III System Design ‣ More with Less: Efficient Parallel Scientific Code Translation via an Agent-Skill Workflow").

|                        |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Skill                  | Core Prompt Content                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| AnalyzerSkill (shared) | System: You are a code analysis assistant. Describe what a program does in plain, framework-independent terms. User: Analyze the following {source_language} code. Focus only on the real execution logic and numerical behavior. Include: what problem the program solves, inputs and expected outputs, computation stages, correctness criteria, and numerical concerns. Do NOT focus on {target_language} API names, {target_language and runtime constructs} or synchronization details. Keep the response under 250 words. |
| MemoryPlanningSkill    | System: You are an expert in {target_language} parallelism. User: Given the following {source_language} code, produce a memory plan for {target_language} execution. List each buffer with: variable name, size, lifetime, and sharing behavior. Identify where reduction, atomic, critical, or barrier clauses are needed. Respond as a bullet list only.                                                                                                                                                                      |
| TranslatorSkill        | \[BEGIN CODE SUMMARY\] {code_summary} \[END CODE SUMMARY\] \[BEGIN MEMORY PLAN\] {memory_plan} \[END MEMORY PLAN\] Generate new code to refactor the following parallelized {source_language} program to instead use C++ code written with {target_language} directives.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| PatchSkill             | The following code was compiled with {compiler} {flags} and produced the following compile error: {compile_log} Re-factor the above code with a fix to eliminate the stated error.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| SemanticRepair         | System: You are a coding assistant that fixes numerical logic errors in {target_language} code. User: The translated code was executed and produced incorrect or unexpected output. Translated stdout: {run_stdout} Translated stderr: {run_stderr} Identify and fix the numerical logic error.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| SyncRepair             | System: You are an expert in {target_language} parallel programming synchronization. User: The following {target_language} code crashes or produces non-deterministic results (exit code {run_exit_code}, stderr: {run_stderr}). Add missing barriers, atomic operations, or reduction clauses as needed.                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| MemoryRepair           | System: You are a coding assistant that fixes memory-related compilation errors in {target_language} code. User: The following code was compiled with {compiler} {flags} and produced a compile error related to memory usage: {compile_log} \[BEGIN MEMORY PLAN\] {memory_plan} \[END MEMORY PLAN\] Fix the memory issue.                                                                                                                                                                                                      |

TABLE II: Core content of skill prompts. Placeholders in braces are
filled at runtime.

The Orchestrator implements the central control loop. It consumes
verdicts, advances the pipeline to the next agent or repair skill, and
enforces termination conditions. The orchestrator also maintains the
unified self-correction budget, configurable at construction time, whose
cap on repair attempts applies across the entire system. Forward
progress through translation, compilation, and execution does not
consume this budget; only repair invocations do. This separation ensures
that successful translations are not penalized by the presence of repair
machinery, while preventing runaway retry loops.

### III-C Agent Skills and Repair Mechanisms

Each agent in the system is composed of one or more core skills that
encapsulate a single capability. Repair skills are managed directly by
the orchestrator and invoked when a stage returns a failure verdict.

The TranslationAgent runs three skills in sequence. First, the
AnalyzerSkill invokes an LLM to produce a framework-independent
functional summary of the source program, describing its computation
stages, inputs, outputs, and correctness criteria. The summary is stored
in the shared state and later consumed by the translator. Then, the
MemoryPlanningSkill generates a memory and data-layout plan for the
target execution model, mapping each buffer to its intended sharing
behavior, lifetime, and synchronization requirements. Finally, the
TranslatorSkill synthesizes the complete target-language program by
combining the source code with the functional summary and the memory
plan.

The CompilationAgent contains two skills. The CompilerSkill invokes the
real target-language compiler and captures the compilation log and the
resulting binary path. If compilation succeeds, the agent returns a pass
verdict and control advances to the ExecutionAgent; otherwise, the
ErrorClassifierSkill applies a set of trigger condition as shown in
Table
[I](#S3.T1 "TABLE I ‣ III-A Overview and Design Goals ‣ III System Design ‣ More with Less: Efficient Parallel Scientific Code Translation via an Agent-Skill Workflow")
to the compiler log as presented in Section
[III-B](#S3.SS2 "III-B Task State, Verdict, and Orchestrator ‣ III System Design ‣ More with Less: Efficient Parallel Scientific Code Translation via an Agent-Skill Workflow").

The ExecutionAgent also contains two skills. The RunnerSkill executes
the compiled binary with test arguments and records stdout, stderr, and
the exit code. The RuntimeAnalysisSkill then maps the recorded output to
a verdict category according to the trigger conditions in
Table [I](#S3.T1 "TABLE I ‣ III-A Overview and Design Goals ‣ III System Design ‣ More with Less: Efficient Parallel Scientific Code Translation via an Agent-Skill Workflow").
If execution times out, the RuntimeAnalysisSkill automatically scales
down numeric test arguments that exceed a configurable threshold. The
scaling factor is halved across attempts, and the modified arguments are
written back to the TaskState before the binary is rerun with smaller
inputs. This mechanism allows computationally intensive kernels to be
validated without manual input tuning. And the total number of rescaling
attempts is configurable and defaults to five.

Four repair skills handle the failure modes exposed by compilation and
execution. Two address compilation failures: the PatchSkill rewrites the
current code to eliminate a reported compilation error, and the
MemoryRepair specializes in memory-related compilation errors, using the
previously generated memory plan to correct allocation, mapping, or
sharing mistakes. The other two repair skills address runtime failures:
the SemanticRepair fixes numerical or logical errors observed at
runtime, such as incorrect loop bounds, missing reductions, or precision
loss, and the SyncRepair addresses crashes and non-deterministic
behavior by inserting missing barriers, atomic operations, or
synchronization constructs. Each repair skill invokes an LLM to generate
corrected code and returns a repair-compilation verdict, sending the
modified code back to the CompilationAgent and closing the
self-correction loop.

The prompts that drive these skills are summarized in
Table [II](#S3.T2 "TABLE II ‣ III-B Task State, Verdict, and Orchestrator ‣ III System Design ‣ More with Less: Efficient Parallel Scientific Code Translation via an Agent-Skill Workflow").
The AnalyzerSkill uses a shared prompt across all translation pairs,
while the TranslatorSkill and repair skills use pair-specific prompts
that follow a common structure but encode different target-model
constraints.

### III-D Compilation, Runtime, and LLM-based Verification

The framework adopts an in-loop verification stage plus an LLM-based
complementary verification. The in-loop verification stage relies on
compiler and runtime feedback to validate translated programs and
provide signals for the self-correction workflow. Compilation success is
treated as the prerequisite for execution, while runtime behavior is
evaluated through execution status and program outputs. A translation is
accepted by this stage only when the generated binary exits with code
zero and its output contains no explicit FAIL marker (a
failure-indicating word in the program output), corresponding to the
EQUIVALENT verdict in
Table [I](#S3.T1 "TABLE I ‣ III-A Overview and Design Goals ‣ III System Design ‣ More with Less: Efficient Parallel Scientific Code Translation via an Agent-Skill Workflow").

Although compiler and runtime verification provide reliable and
reproducible signals, they cannot capture all correctness issues in
translated programs. A program may compile successfully and terminate
normally while still failing to execute the intended workload, producing
incomplete computations, or generating incorrect numerical results
without explicit error messages. Such false positives can lead to an
overestimation of translation success rates and obscure the actual
capability of the translation framework.

To address these limitations, we introduce an LLM-based complementary
verification. Unlike the compiler and runtime checks that participate
directly in the self-correction workflow, the LLM verifier is applied
offline to cached translation artifacts and aims to identify defects
that escape compiler and runtime checks. The verifier receives the
complete source program and execution outputs, and produces a structured
JSON judgment based on a predefined evaluation rubric. Its role is
therefore evaluative rather than corrective: it provides a stricter
post-hoc assessment of translation quality without altering the
translations it audits. In practice, its confidence scores can guide
users in prioritizing artifacts for manual inspection, starting with the
least confident ones.

The verifier follows several decision criteria:

1.  1.  The translated program must genuinely execute the intended benchmark
        workload rather than bypassing computation through early exits,
        placeholder implementations, or no-op kernels;
2.  2.  Explicit failure indicators or non-zero error counts in the
        execution output are treated as definitive failures, regardless of
        superficial success signals;
3.  3.  Numerical discrepancies are evaluated based on semantic correctness
        rather than strict textual matching, allowing legitimate
        floating-point variations;
4.  4.  Surface-level success markers (e.g., “PASS”) are considered
        insufficient unless supported by meaningful execution traces and
        consistent computational results;
5.  5.  Empty, truncated, or otherwise unverifiable outputs are
        conservatively classified as failures to avoid rewarding silent
        crashes or incomplete executions.

In addition to a binary pass/fail judgment, the verifier reports a
confidence score in the interval $`[0,1]`$. The confidence score is
calibrated using a five-tier rubric that maps the strength of available
evidence to numerical ranges:

1.  1.  0.95–1.0: The execution output contains explicit verification
        evidence (e.g., PASS markers, zero failures, or low RMSE), and the
        translated program is complete;
2.  2.  0.8–0.9: The output appears correct, but the verification evidence
        is incomplete or partially documented;
3.  3.  0.6–0.7: Execution succeeds, but explicit verification signals are
        absent and the judgment relies primarily on program analysis;
4.  4.  0.4–0.5: The available evidence is weak or contradictory, making the
        judgment uncertain;
5.  5.  0.0–0.3: The available information is insufficient for a reliable
        assessment.

By introducing this LLM-based complementary verification, the framework
reduces the risk of overestimating translation quality due to
limitations of compiler and runtime checks. The confidence-aware
evaluation further encourages conservative judgments in ambiguous cases
and provides a more reliable assessment of generated parallel programs.

## IV Evaluation

### IV-A Experimental Setup

##### Benchmarks

We evaluate our approach on HeCBench \[[19](#bib.bib32)\], a widely-used
benchmark collection of HPC and AI kernels written in CUDA, OpenMP, SYCL
and HIP. It provides a diverse set of real-world GPU workloads that
allow us to assess cross-model code translation in terms of correctness
and token usage. In our experiments, we select a representative subset
of 30 benchmarks from HeCBench for domain coverage rather than language
completeness, spanning a wide range of application domains
(Table [III](#S4.T3 "TABLE III ‣ Environment and Configuration ‣ IV-A Experimental Setup ‣ IV Evaluation ‣ More with Less: Efficient Parallel Scientific Code Translation via an Agent-Skill Workflow"));
requiring implementations in all three programming models would skew the
subset toward older and simpler kernels. Six of the selected kernels
lack OpenMP implementations, leaving 24 benchmarks per OpenMP-source
direction.

##### Models, directions, and baseline

We conduct experiments with three recent open-source LLMs
(DeepSeek-V4-Flash \[[40](#bib.bib38)\], GLM-5.2 \[[41](#bib.bib40)\],
and Kimi-K2.7-Code \[[42](#bib.bib39)\]) on all six directed language
pairs among CUDA, OpenMP, and SYCL. We compare our framework with
LASSI \[[13](#bib.bib13)\]: to keep the comparison fair, we replace the
LLMs used in the original LASSI study (GPT-4, Codestral, WizardCoder,
and DeepSeek-Coder-V2) with the same three LLMs, and run both systems on
the same benchmark set under identical compilation and execution
environments.

##### Environment and Configuration

We use g++ 8.5.0 for OpenMP target programs, nvcc 12.8 for CUDA target
programs, and icpx/dpcpp 2021.4.0 for SYCL target programs. Compilation
is capped at 300 seconds and execution at 120 seconds. The repair loop
permits up to 9 iterations.

### IV-B Correctness and Token Consumption Evaluation among OpenMP, CUDA, and SYCL

Table [IV](#S4.T4 "TABLE IV ‣ Environment and Configuration ‣ IV-A Experimental Setup ‣ IV Evaluation ‣ More with Less: Efficient Parallel Scientific Code Translation via an Agent-Skill Workflow")
reports, for every system, model, and direction, the verified
correctness rate together with the total token consumption and its
translation and repair split. We start with DeepSeek V4 Flash on the
CUDA$`\leftrightarrow`$OpenMP pair, the most common translation scenario
in HPC practice and also the pair LASSI was originally designed for.
Both systems perform well here: our framework translates 93.3%
(CUDA$`\rightarrow`$OpenMP) and 95.8% (OpenMP$`\rightarrow`$CUDA) of the
benchmarks correctly, against LASSI’s 86.7% and 87.5%. The two systems
differ mainly in how much they spend and where the tokens go. LASSI
consumes 1,327k and 1,058k tokens on the two directions, of which 41%
and 56% go into repairing retrieval-based drafts. Our framework consumes
718k and 835k tokens, 45.9% and 21.1% less, with only 28% and 47% spent
on repair.

Beyond the CUDA$`\leftrightarrow`$OpenMP pair LASSI was designed for, we
add SYCL as a representative low-resource parallel programming model and
extend the evaluation to all six directions with the same model. Our
framework attains the higher correctness rate on every direction and
averages 88.7% against LASSI’s 65.5%. The gap is smallest on
SYCL$`\rightarrow`$CUDA (93.3% vs. 83.3%), where both systems can rely
on the model’s familiarity with CUDA-style code, and largest on
OpenMP$`\rightarrow`$SYCL (79.2% vs. 33.3%), where LASSI’s retrieval
corpus offers little reusable material. Runs with SYCL as the target are
intrinsically harder for both systems, averaging 74.6% for our framework
and 40.0% for LASSI against 96.7% and 68.3% with SYCL as the source,
while the CUDA$`\leftrightarrow`$OpenMP pair is nearly symmetric (93.3%
vs. 95.8%). Both systems read low-resource SYCL far better than they
write it. The average token consumption is 26.2% lower at the same time
(1,071k vs. 1,451k per direction). The only direction where our
framework spends more is SYCL$`\rightarrow`$CUDA (1,191k vs. 1,174k,
+1.5%), and there the extra repair rounds come with a 10.0% correctness
gain. Beyond these direction-level trends, the failing benchmarks show
no obvious pattern, scattering across domains and kernel styles.

### IV-C Generalization Across Models

The remaining rows of
Table [IV](#S4.T4 "TABLE IV ‣ Environment and Configuration ‣ IV-A Experimental Setup ‣ IV Evaluation ‣ More with Less: Efficient Parallel Scientific Code Translation via an Agent-Skill Workflow")
repeat the experiment with GLM-5.2 and Kimi-K2.7-Code, and the key
observation is that the performance of our framework is largely agnostic
to the choice of LLM. Its per-model averages span only 16.0% (78.6% to
94.6%), and every direction stays from 6.7% to 33.3% across models
(17.0% on average), because the verify-and-repair loop compensates for
weaker first drafts instead of relying on a particular model’s
strengths. LASSI, by comparison, fluctuates far more: 31.0% across its
per-model averages and 38.5% per direction, with swings of 27.5% to
40.0% even on its three strongest directions. Our framework also attains
the higher correctness rate in all 18 combinations. Token consumption is
equally predictable, staying within 1,018k to 1,115k tokens per
direction (a spread below 10%; LASSI: 1,445k to 2,341k), 29.5% to 52.4%
below LASSI per model; only two of the 18 cells spend more than LASSI,
and both buy large correctness gains (up to +60.0% for +24.5% tokens).

To isolate the contribution of the repair loop,
Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Fig. 2 ‣ Environment and Configuration ‣ IV-A Experimental Setup ‣ IV Evaluation ‣ More with Less: Efficient Parallel Scientific Code Translation via an Agent-Skill Workflow")
follows six representative model and direction combinations through the
loop, plotting the cumulative token consumption (bars, left axis) and
the cumulative success rate (curve, right axis) after each round, where

both systems (70.8% for our framework and 21.1% for LASSI), and shows it
under all three models. All three start at or below 12.5%, and the
success rate climbs steadily as the loop accumulates tokens, reaching
79.2%, 58.3%, and 75.0% within nine repairs: gains of 50.0% to 70.9%
that come entirely from verification-guided repair rather than from the
first draft. The bottom row varies the direction for DeepSeek V4 Flash.
On the easier CUDA$`\leftrightarrow`$OpenMP pair the strong first drafts

CUDA$`\rightarrow`$SYCL it adds 60.0% to reach 70.0%. In all six panels

showing that the repair loop, not the initial generation, accounts for

### IV-E LLM-based Complementary Verification

All success rates reported so far are judged by the simple in-loop
verification stage, which compiles each artifact, runs it, and checks
its output. To assess how much these judgments can be trusted, we
additionally applied the rigorous LLM-based complementary verification
(Section [III-D](#S3.SS4 "III-D Compilation, Runtime, and LLM-based Verification ‣ III System Design ‣ More with Less: Efficient Parallel Scientific Code Translation via an Agent-Skill Workflow")),
backed by DeepSeek V4 Flash, to the cached artifacts of both systems.
The verifier issues a pass or fail judgment together with a confidence
score;
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Fig. 3 ‣ IV-E LLM-based Complementary Verification ‣ IV Evaluation ‣ More with Less: Efficient Parallel Scientific Code Translation via an Agent-Skill Workflow")
shows the confidence distribution over the 999 artifacts that produced
output (1,008 runs in total, minus 9 LASSI runs with Kimi K2.7 Code
where, due to the complexity of the tasks, the model repeatedly failed
to complete its output within the API time limit).

compares the pass rates under the two verification stages. The rigorous
complementary verification lowers the pass rates of both systems, by
8.3% to 17.3% for our framework and by 6.5% to 19.1% for LASSI, and it
finds no false negatives: no artifact rejected in the loop is accepted
by the verifier. Under the stricter check our framework still passes
71.4%, 68.5%, and 86.3% of its artifacts with the three models, keeping
margins of 25.0%, 40.5%, and 37.2% over LASSI. In total, 117 artifacts
(11.7%) are false positives of the in-loop stage, and
Table [VI](#S4.T6 "TABLE VI ‣ IV-E LLM-based Complementary Verification ‣ IV Evaluation ‣ More with Less: Efficient Parallel Scientific Code Translation via an Agent-Skill Workflow")
groups them into eight escape modes led by placeholder implementations
(31 cases), numerical errors (28), and skipped verification (25). The
verifier is confident in most of its judgments: the median confidence is
0.95, 79.3% of the judgments score at least 0.9, and only 57 artifacts
(5.7%) fall below 0.8, so manual spot-checking of the uncertain
remainder stays feasible. Combining the stricter pass rates with token
consumption, our framework spends 46k to 54k tokens per verified
successful benchmark across the three models, against 112k to 184k for
LASSI, a 2.1 to 3.9 times advantage in cost per verified success.

## V Discussion

The experiments and the design process itself yield the following
findings about LLM-based translation of parallel programs under
verification-guided repair.

1.  1.  Skills make both translation and repair more token-efficient.
        Analysis and memory-planning skills target translation at an
        explicit parallelization plan rather than a loosely matching
        retrieved example, and verification-classified feedback targets
        repair at the diagnosed defect rather than blind regeneration,
        keeping the repair share of the budget smaller across all models and
        directions.
2.  2.  Translation difficulty is determined by the target model, not the
        source. Directions with the same target cluster together in
        correctness, with low-resource SYCL consistently the hardest target:
        current LLMs read low-resource parallel code far better than they
        write it, which is also why retrieval offers little help on such
        directions.
3.  3.  The repair loop accounts for most of the final correctness, but
        returns diminish beyond roughly five rounds. Success climbs
        monotonically from a low round-0 base on hard directions and still
        adds large gains on easy pairs, with most gains arriving within five
        rounds; later rounds mostly accumulate tokens. First-draft strength
        determines what a direction costs, not how many benchmarks
        eventually pass, and failures that survive many rounds are
        systematic ones that generous iteration caps cannot fix.
4.  4.  Verification and repair make the framework largely model-agnostic.
        Correctness and token consumption stay in narrow bands across models
        while the retrieval-based baseline swings widely on both; the loop
        compensates for weaker first drafts, so framework-level mechanisms
        matter more than the choice of LLM.
5.  5.  Compiler and runtime checks are necessary but not sufficient.
        In-loop verification overestimates the success of both systems, with
        systematic escapes led by placeholder implementations, weakened
        validation, and silent numerical errors. The complementary
        verification adds no false negatives and preserves the margins
        between systems, and its calibrated confidence concentrates at the
        high end, leaving only a small uncertain tail for manual
        spot-checking.
6.  6.  Separating generation, failure classification, and repair keeps
        self-correction bounded. Verdict routing gives each repair skill a
        single failure mode and the context it needs, and the unified budget
        prevents runaway retries without penalizing clean runs; the same
        encapsulation makes the framework direction-agnostic.

## VI Conclusion and Future Work

This paper presented a multi-agent system for parallel scientific code
translation, motivated by two gaps in existing pipelines: they verify
correctness against criteria that do not match scientific computing
practice, and they spend token budgets on blind, undifferentiated
retries. Our framework separates translation, compilation diagnosis, and
execution validation into three agents coordinated by a verdict-driven
orchestrator, routes each diagnosed failure to a targeted repair skill,
and treats automated output checking as a first-class validation step.
On 30 HeCBench kernels translated bidirectionally among OpenMP, CUDA,
and SYCL with three recent open-source LLMs, our framework attains the
higher verified correctness rate in all 18 model and direction
combinations over LASSI, with per-model averages of 78.6% to 94.6%
against 34.5% to 65.5%, while consuming 29.5% to 52.4% fewer tokens.
Under the stricter LLM-based complementary verification, it preserves
margins of 25.0% to 40.5% at a 2.1 to 3.9 times advantage in cost per
verified success. The experiments further show that the repair loop
accounts for most of the final correctness; verification-guided repair
makes the framework largely model-agnostic; and compiler and runtime
checks alone systematically overestimate translation success. More
capable translation behavior, in other words, comes not from more
expensive prompting but from better verification scaffolding around the
model.

Several challenges remain open. First, our evaluation is limited to
kernel-level benchmarks; extending the framework to multi-file codebases
and full applications will require cross-file analysis, build-system
awareness, and translation state that persists across compilation units.
Second, the LLM-based complementary verification can itself be
strengthened, for example through refined evaluation rubrics,
multi-verifier voting, and tighter coupling between confidence scores
and targeted re-execution, so that the uncertain tail requiring manual
inspection shrinks further. Third, correctness is only the first step
toward practical porting: we plan to incorporate performance feedback
into the repair loop so that translated programs are not only
numerically correct but also performant, and to extend the
direction-agnostic skill mechanism to further programming models such as
HIP and Kokkos, where the low-resource difficulty observed for SYCL
targets is likely to be even more pronounced.

Appendix: Artifact Description/Artifact Evaluation

Artifact Description (AD)

## VII Overview of Contributions and Artifacts

### VII-A Paper’s Main Contributions

$`C_{1}`$  
A multi-agent framework for automated HPC code translation across CUDA,
OpenMP, and SYCL, comprising a TranslationAgent, a CompilationAgent, and
an ExecutionAgent coordinated by a verdict-driven Orchestrator.

$`C_{2}`$  
A set of repair skills (Patch, Semantic, Sync, Memory) that detect and
fix compilation, runtime, and correctness errors during translation,
enabling iterative self-correction without human intervention.

$`C_{3}`$  
An evaluation of the framework on 30 HeCBench benchmarks across six
translation directions and three LLM backends (DeepSeek V4 Flash, GLM
5.2, Kimi K2.7 Code), demonstrating higher verified correctness and
lower token consumption than the LASSI baseline.

### VII-B Computational Artifacts

$`A_{1}`$  
https://github.com/dinglhmds/More-with-Less-Efficient-Parallel-Scientific-Code-Translation-via-an-Agent-Skill-Workflow

|             |                       |                |
| ----------- | --------------------- | -------------- |
| Artifact ID | Contributions         | Related        |
|             | Supported             | Paper Elements |
| $`A_{1}`$   | $`C_{1},C_{2},C_{3}`$ | Tables IV–VI   |
|             |                       | Figures 2–3    |

## VIII Artifact Identification

### VIII-A Computational Artifact $`A_{1}`$

### Relation To Contributions

The artifact implements the full multi-agent translation pipeline
described in $`C_{1}`$ and $`C_{2}`$, including the Orchestrator, all
three agents, all repair skills, and the offline LLM-based complementary
verifier. It also contains the LASSI baseline (configured with the same
three LLMs), the batch runner, and the evaluation scripts used to
produce the results in $`C_{3}`$.

### Expected Results

Running the batch evaluation on the 30 HeCBench benchmarks (six
translation directions, three LLMs, both systems) should produce
per-benchmark verdicts (success/failure), token consumption reports,
cumulative success-rate curves, and complementary-verification judgments
matching Tables IV–VI and Figures 2–3 in the paper. The framework is
expected to achieve a higher verified correctness rate than the LASSI
baseline while consuming fewer LLM tokens on average.

### Expected Reproduction Time (in Minutes)

Artifact Setup: approximately 30 minutes (install Python dependencies
and configure LLM API access). Artifact Execution: approximately 8–12
hours for all 30 benchmarks on a GPU cluster (dominated by LLM API
latency). Artifact Analysis: approximately 15 minutes (aggregate
per-benchmark result.json files into summary tables and plots).

### Artifact Setup (incl. Inputs)

#### Hardware

A GPU cluster managed by Slurm with at least one NVIDIA GPU node is
required for executing CUDA baselines and OpenMP/SYCL offload targets.
CPU-only OpenMP execution is also supported as a fallback. The
evaluation used a Slurm cluster with the mrigpu partition (one GPU per
job).

#### Software

- •
  Python 3.9 or newer: https://www.python.org
- •
  OpenAI Python client ($`\geq`$1.0):
  https://github.com/openai/openai-python
- •
  PyYAML ($`\geq`$6.0): https://pyyaml.org
- •
  python-dotenv ($`\geq`$1.0):
  https://github.com/theskumar/python-dotenv
- •
  g++ 8.5.0: https://gcc.gnu.org
- •
  CUDA Toolkit 12.8 (nvcc): https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-toolkit
- •
  Intel oneAPI DPC++/C++ Compiler 2021.4.0 (icpx/dpcpp):
  https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/developer/tools/oneapi/dpc-compiler.html
- •
  Clang/LLVM 18.1.8 (optional, for OpenMP GPU offload):
  https://clang.llvm.org
- •
  Access to an OpenAI-compatible LLM API (DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, or
  equivalent)

#### Datasets / Inputs

The evaluation uses 30 benchmarks selected from HeCBench
(https://github.com/zjin-lcf/HECBench), covering image processing, deep
learning, mathematical and statistical kernels, sorting and parallel
primitives, stencil and numerical methods, hashing, physics simulation,
and signal processing. The selected benchmark names are listed in
DEFAULT_BENCHMARKS in batch_runner.py; the suite itself is obtained by
cloning the HeCBench repository and passing its src directory to the
batch runner via --benchmark-dir. Six of the selected kernels lack
OpenMP implementations, leaving 24 benchmarks per OpenMP-source
direction. No other external datasets are required.

#### Installation and Deployment

Clone the repository, create a Python virtual environment, and install
dependencies:

```ltx_verbatim
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

Configure the LLM API endpoint by copying .env.example to .env and
setting BASE_URL, API_KEY, and MODEL_NAME.

Set environment variables for compilation and execution:

```ltx_verbatim
export CT_CUDA_PATH=/path/to/cuda/12.8
# optional, for OpenMP GPU offload:
export CT_CLANG_HOME=/path/to/llvm/18.1.8
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=\
    $CT_CLANG_HOME/lib:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH
export CT_SLURM_PARTITION=mrigpu
export CT_SLURM_GRES=gpu:1
```

### Artifact Execution

The experiment workflow consists of four tasks: $`T_{1}`$ (translation)
$`\rightarrow`$ $`T_{2}`$ (compilation/execution) $`\rightarrow`$
$`T_{3}`$ (result aggregation) $`\rightarrow`$ $`T_{4}`$ (offline
complementary verification). The full evaluation matrix comprises two
systems (our framework and the LASSI baseline), three LLMs, and six
translation directions; individual runs are independent and can be
distributed across Slurm jobs.

$`T_{1}`$: The batch runner (batch_runner.py) discovers benchmarks under
the HeCBench source directory, reads each source program, and runs the
multi-agent pipeline. The Orchestrator coordinates Analyzer,
MemoryPlanning, and Translator skills to produce target code, then
invokes the CompilationAgent and the ExecutionAgent. If compilation or
execution fails, repair skills mutate the code and the pipeline
re-enters from the corresponding stage. Each benchmark is capped at 300
seconds for compilation, 120 seconds for execution, and a maximum of 9
repair iterations.

$`T_{2}`$: Each source program is compiled with its native compiler
(nvcc -O3 -std=c++17 for CUDA, g++ -O2 -fopenmp -std=c++17 for OpenMP,
icpx -fsycl -std=c++17 for SYCL) and executed on a Slurm GPU node to
obtain reference outputs. Translated programs are compiled with the
corresponding target compiler (for OpenMP GPU offload, clang++ -O3
-fopenmp -fopenmp-targets=nvptx64 -std=c++17) and executed with the same
input arguments.

$`T_{3}`$: Per-benchmark results are written to
output/\<timestamp\>/\<benchmark\>/result.json, containing the verdict,
retry counts, elapsed time, and token usage broken down by category and
repair round. A summary script aggregates these files into the tables
and figures reported in the paper.

$`T_{4}`$: The offline LLM-based complementary verifier is applied to
the cached artifacts of both systems. Given the complete source program
and the execution outputs of a translated program, it produces a
structured JSON judgment (pass/fail plus a confidence score in
$`[0,1]`$) following the rubric described in the paper. Aggregating
these judgments yields the complementary-verification pass rates in
Table V, the false-positive taxonomy in Table VI, and the confidence
distribution in Figure 3.

### Artifact Analysis (incl. Outputs)

The expected output is a set of per-benchmark result.json files,
per-artifact verification judgments, and a summary report. The key
metrics are: (1) the verified correctness rate (the EQUIVALENT verdict,
routed to the terminal Done state), (2) token consumption aggregated by
direction and model, (3) the cumulative success rate as a function of
repair rounds, and (4) the complementary-verification pass rates and
confidence distribution. These correspond to Tables IV–VI and Figures
2–3 in the paper.

Artifact Evaluation (AE)

### VIII-A Computational Artifact $`A_{1}`$

### Artifact Setup (incl. Inputs)

Access. The artifact is available at
https://github.com/dinglhmds/More-with-Less-Efficient-Parallel-Scientific-Code-Translation-via-an-Agent-Skill-Workflow.
Reviewers are granted access to an OpenAI-compatible LLM endpoint; the
endpoint URL and an API key with sufficient quota are provided through
the submission system.

Hardware. One NVIDIA GPU node on a Slurm-managed cluster (one GPU per
job), as described in the AD Appendix.

Software. Python 3.9+ with the packages listed in requirements.txt
(OpenAI client, PyYAML, python-dotenv); g++ 8.5.0, CUDA Toolkit 12.8,
and Intel oneAPI DPC++/C++ Compiler 2021.4.0. Exact installation
commands and environment variables are given in the AD Appendix
(Artifact Setup) and in the repository README.md.

### Artifact Execution

To stay within the evaluation time budget, we define a reduced but
representative evaluation: the CUDA$`\rightarrow`$OpenMP direction with
DeepSeek V4 Flash, all 30 benchmarks, run for both our framework and the
LASSI baseline. This reproduces one column pair of Table IV and the
bottom-left panel of Figure 2. The model is selected via MODEL_NAME in
.env.

$`E_{1}`$ (translation with self-correction): for our framework, run

```ltx_verbatim
export CT_TRANSLATION_DIRECTION=\
    cuda_to_openmp
python batch_runner.py \
    --benchmark-dir <hecbench>/src \
    --output batch_cuda2omp_ae.json \
    --no-context --no-rag \
    --use-memory-plan \
    --auto-scale-on-timeout \
    --max-retries 5
```

and for the LASSI baseline, run

```ltx_verbatim
python experiments/lassi/\
    run_lassi30_cuda2omp_context.py
```

(On a Slurm cluster, the equivalent submission scripts are
scripts/submit*framework_cuda_to_openmp_norag_nocontext.sh and
scripts/submit_lassi_cuda2omp_context.sh; adapt the cluster-specific
paths before use.) For each benchmark this executes tasks $`T*{1}`$ and
$`T\_{2}`$ of the AD workflow: the verdict-driven translation loop,
compilation with g++ -O2 -fopenmp -std=c++17, and execution on the GPU
node, capped at 300 s compilation, 120 s execution, and 9 repair
iterations.

$`E_{2}`$ (aggregation): run

```ltx_verbatim
python tools/\
    framework_model_direction_summary.py
python tools/framework_round_summary.py
```

which aggregate all result.json files into a summary table and the
cumulative success-rate data (task $`T_{3}`$).

Optionally, $`E_{3}`$ (complementary verification): run

```ltx_verbatim
python tools/run_llm_verdict_full.py
```

to apply the offline LLM-based verifier (task $`T_{4}`$) to the cached
artifacts, producing per-artifact pass/fail judgments with confidence
scores.

### Artifact Analysis (incl. Outputs)

Expected results. $`E_{1}`$ produces 30 result.json files per system;
$`E_{2}`$ prints a table with the verified correctness rate and total
token consumption per system, together with the cumulative success-rate
curve over repair rounds.

Evaluation methodology. Compare the summary table against the
CUDA$`\rightarrow`$OpenMP columns of Table IV: our framework should
achieve a higher verified correctness rate than LASSI (paper: 93.3% vs.
86.7%) at lower token consumption (paper: 718k vs. 1,327k). Because LLM
outputs are nondeterministic, absolute rates may shift by a few
percentage points between runs; the reproduction criterion is that the
ordering of the two systems and the approximate split of tokens between
translation and repair are preserved. The cumulative curve should
increase monotonically, matching the bottom-left panel of Figure 2.

Correlation with contributions. Successful completion of the
verdict-driven loop, including repair invocations, substantiates
$`C_{1}`$ and $`C_{2}`$; the correctness and token comparison between
the two systems substantiates $`C_{3}`$. If $`E_{3}`$ is executed, the
verifier’s judgments additionally provide the stricter complementary
pass rates underlying Table V.
